name: EGCG

lead: EGCG is the most abundant catechin in green tea, sold as a concentrated extract in fat-burner and pre-workout products. Users take it for a small extra calorie burn and slightly lower body fat.

It may modestly raise energy expenditure and fat oxidation by prolonging noradrenaline signalling and may reduce fat absorption in the gut. Trials and meta-analyses of green tea catechins show small effects on weight and fat mass, varying with caffeine intake and baseline habits. Some users speculate about muscle effects via myostatin, an idea based on lab findings.

paras: It is taken as a capsule or extract, often before workouts and combined with caffeine-based thermogenics and L-carnitine. Brewed green tea is another route.

Concentrated extracts, especially on an empty stomach, have been linked to rare liver injury; in 2018 the European Food Safety Authority said 800 mg or more daily from supplements could raise liver-damage risk. The FDA issued warning letters to EGCG supplement makers between 2008 and 2017. It can reduce iron absorption and interact with some drugs. Brewed tea is considered safe.

chain: Green tea catechin raises metabolism slightly
angle.text: EGCG is a green tea extract taken as a fat burner, where a slightly higher metabolism adds a small extra calorie burn and slightly lower body fat. Studies show small thermogenic effects with mixed results; the muscle-building talk comes from lab findings and users.

lead: Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG, epigallocatechin-3-gallate) is the most abundant catechin in tea, an ester of epigallocatechin and gallic acid. It occurs at high levels in dried green tea leaves (about 7,380 mg per 100 g), in white tea, and in smaller amounts in black tea, and it is sold in concentrated form in green tea extracts and many dietary supplements.[1]

In physique and fat-loss circles EGCG is taken as a fat-burner or pre-workout ingredient, often alongside caffeine-based thermogenics and L-carnitine, with the aim of getting leaner and showing more muscle definition; some forum users have also speculated about effects on myostatin.[2][3][4][5][6] The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health says catechins combined with caffeine may have a modest effect on body weight, with results depending on the product and the person's activity level.[7] Wikipedia's green tea extract article, by contrast, states that there is no good evidence that green tea aids weight loss or weight maintenance.[8]

EGCG is also one of the most heavily studied plant compounds in the laboratory, with reported effects on inflammation, cell signalling, protein aggregation and cancer cell lines, and its main prescription-drug use comes from a green tea extract ointment approved in the US in 2006.[1][9][10] Safety at high supplement intakes is a documented concern: the European Food Safety Authority stated in 2018 that a daily intake of 800 mg or more of EGCG from supplements could raise the risk of liver damage, and the US FDA issued warning letters to EGCG supplement makers between 2008 and 2017.[1][11]

paras: EGCG extracts are marketed for fat loss and metabolic support. T Nation posters suggest taking an EGCG extract before training, sometimes with a thermogenic fat-burner or alongside L-carnitine after a meal, or using it during structured diets such as the Velocity Diet, and a supplement maker's page lists it among products for cellular, cardiovascular and metabolic health.[2][3][4][12] In one fat-loss thread a poster described it as an optional add-on after diet: 'EGCG pre workput and L-carnitine with post workout meal', placed after cutting junk food and monitoring carbohydrates.[3]

The appearance goal is a lower body-fat percentage and more visible muscle. The proposed route is that catechins, particularly together with caffeine, nudge energy expenditure and fat use upward; NCCIH summarises the weight effect as modest.[7]

Green tea is the main dietary source, with about 70.2 mg of EGCG per 100 mL of brewed tea, roughly 165 mg per cup, and trace amounts occur in apple skin, plums, onions, hazelnuts and pecans.[1] Black tea processing converts most catechins into theaflavins and thearubigins, so black tea contains much less.[1] Supplements come as liquids, powders, capsules and tablets, and some extracts contain large amounts of caffeine, up to 17.4% of their weight according to Wikipedia.[8]

Laboratory and clinical interest covers cancer prevention, inflammation, neurodegeneration and skin conditions, among others. Reviews summarise catechin effects on health, cancer and inflammation, and trials have examined topical EGCG in vitiligo and green tea extract for preventing colorectal adenomas.[13][14][15][16][17] A green tea extract ointment (sinecatechins, sold as Veregen and Polyphenon E), whose catechins are about 55% EGCG, was approved by the FDA in 2006 as a prescription botanical drug for genital warts, the first botanical drug the agency approved.[10][8]

EGCG has the formula C22H18O11 and a molar mass of 458.372 g/mol, and dissolves at about 5 g/L in water and about 20 g/L in ethanol, according to Wikipedia.[1] It belongs to the flavan-3-ol family of catechins, the group named after catechu, a tannic extract of Acacia catechu, and found in tea, cocoa, grapes and pome fruits.[18]

After oral intake EGCG levels in blood peak within about 1.7 hours, with an absorbed plasma half-life of around 5 hours and most unchanged EGCG excreted in urine within about 8 hours. Methylated metabolites have longer half-lives and reach 8 to 25 times the plasma levels of unmetabolised EGCG.[1] Wikipedia reports that oral absorption is poor even at intakes equivalent to 8 to 16 cups of green tea a day, an amount that can cause nausea or heartburn.[1]

In laboratory work EGCG has been reported to inhibit NF-kappa-B-dependent inflammatory signalling, inhibit DNA methyltransferase in cancer cell lines, remodel amyloid and alpha-synuclein fibrils, scavenge radicals and activate AMPK, among many other effects whose relevance to people taking oral supplements is uncertain given low absorption.[19][9][20][21][22]

A 2016 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (NCT02147041) tested high-dose green tea extract providing 856.8 mg of EGCG daily in 102 women with central obesity, with outcomes including weight, lipid profile and obesity-related hormone peptides.[23] A 2016 review cited by Wikipedia found that daily doses of 107 to 856 mg over four to 14 weeks produced a small reduction in LDL cholesterol, whereas a 2011 EFSA analysis could not establish a cause-and-effect link between tea catechins and normal LDL levels.[1] NCCIH reports that green tea extract modestly lowered total and LDL cholesterol with no effect on HDL or triglycerides.[7]

A 2018 randomized trial in 38 untrained men examined a 28-day proprietary Camellia sinensis polyphenol blend and apoptotic signalling in muscle biopsies after acute resistance exercise, reporting that supplementation altered signalling; it measured cell-signalling markers, not muscle size.[24] A 2022 randomized trial tested green tea extract for preventing colorectal adenomas, and a 2021 trial tested topical EGCG in vitiligo.[14][15] Registered trials cover esophageal cancer symptoms, radiotherapy-related esophagitis, colorectal cancer chemoprevention, Down syndrome cognition and foetal alcohol syndrome, among others; an insulin-response trial in obesity and hypertension was registered but withdrawn.[25][26][27][28]
No published trial of EGCG in healthy lifters has established an effect on myostatin or muscle mass.

A 2018 review concluded that excessive intake may cause liver toxicity, and EFSA concluded in 2018 that 800 mg or more per day could increase the risk of liver damage; the same sources describe 338 mg per day as considered safe in capsule form and 704 mg per day as safe when consumed as tea.[1][11] A United States Pharmacopeia review also examined the hepatotoxicity of green tea extracts, and a 2018 review examined the safety of green tea and extract consumption in adults.[29][30] EFSA considers traditionally prepared green tea safe, with liver injury rare.[8]

NCCIH reports that extract supplements may cause nausea, constipation, abdominal discomfort and higher blood pressure; that liver injury is uncommon but has been reported mainly with extract tablets and capsules; and that people with a certain immune-related gene variant, found in 5 to 15 percent of Americans, appear more susceptible.[7] It also lists drug interactions, including reduced effectiveness of nadolol at high doses, lower atorvastatin levels, and an interaction with raloxifene.[7] Wikipedia adds that green tea can interfere with the chemotherapy drug bortezomib, and that a 2020 Cochrane review reported gastrointestinal upset, insomnia, raised blood pressure and skin reactions as possible effects of extracts.[8]
A T Nation poster notes that tea-derived products can cause morning nausea on an empty stomach.[31]

Between 2008 and 2017 the FDA sent several warning letters to makers of EGCG supplements, mostly for promoting them as treating or preventing diseases, which classifies them as unapproved new drugs, and one for inadequate quality assurance and labelling.[1] In 2017 Health Canada recommended a warning label on green tea extract and suggested limiting it to adults, and in 2018 EFSA issued its scientific opinion on green tea catechin safety.[8][11] In the US, other green tea products are generally sold as dietary supplements, which are not FDA-approved before sale, and manufacturers are responsible for their safety and labelling.[7]

sections.h: Use in fitness and looksmaxxing communities
paras: EGCG appears mostly in bodybuilding and fat-loss forums rather than looksmaxxing forums. On T Nation it is mentioned as one ingredient in fat-loss and diet-support routines, often with caffeine-based thermogenics, and the thread titles include Velocity Diet support, best fat-loss regimens and belly-fat supplements.[2][3][4] A 2007-2008 T Nation thread titled 'Wow! EGCG and Myostatin' debated a laboratory report on Smad signalling; one poster cited it as a possible natural myostatin inhibitor, another called the idea unlikely because many people use EGCG without noticeable muscle gains, and a later post corrected the dosing arithmetic, noting poor oral bioavailability so that mouse-level doses seemed to require injection.[6] The thread did not produce direct human evidence.[6]
The product is also commonly discussed as a general-health supplement, and a supplement maker's wish-list thread on the same forum mentions EGCG among requested products.[12][32]

A 2008 paper in Nature Structural and Molecular Biology reported EGCG redirecting amyloidogenic polypeptides into unstructured, off-pathway oligomers, and 2010 work reported remodelling of alpha-synuclein and amyloid-beta fibrils.[21][22] Wikipedia's catechin article notes that catechins are heavily metabolised during digestion, which complicates the mechanism behind reported blood-pressure effects.[18]

lore.intro: In bodybuilding forums EGCG is treated as a fat-burner and general-health supplement, and a 2007-2008 thread speculated about myostatin inhibition; supplement makers promote concentrated EGCG for health support.[2][3][4][12][6]
